name: death
sources: Cunliffe, Barry. The Ancient Celts. Oxford: Oxford University Press, 1997. pp. 208 ff.
Dorson, Richard M., ed. Peasant Customs and Savage Myths: Selections from the British Folklorists. Vol. II. Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1968, 29.
MacCulloch, J. A. The Religion of the Ancient Celts. London: Constable, 1911, pp. 165 ff.
Ross, Anne. Folklore of the Scottish Highlands. London: B. T. Batsford, Ltd., 1976, 40.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The Celtic idea of death was a cosmological concept. Archaeological evidence points to permeable boundaries between this world and the next. Places such as the hearth and the burial ground were seen as openings where the dead could reenter this world. Caesar wrote that the continental Celts believed in reincarnation. Other writers of his era claimed the bravery of Celtic warriors came from their faith that they would fight again. Scholars dispute whether this was real Celtic belief. Burial practices offer evidence of Celtic views on death. In the late centuries B.C.E., the continental Celts buried their dead with grave goods such as mirrors and weapons. Some of the greatest archaeological finds come from these early graves. Later, the Celts turned to cremation, burning the bodies of their dead. It is unknown whether this marked a change in belief or an adoption of Roman custom. Among insular Celts there is no evidence of burial before the first century B.C.E., which suggests cremation or excarnation, the exposure of the body. Myth also hints that some remains, especially the head, were preserved, notably for warriors killed in battle. The dead did not occupy a separate realm like the Christian Heaven or Hell. They kept a relationship with those left behind. That relationship could be happy or destructive, depending on the events of physical life. In the Scottish Highlands, the dead could return to wreak vengeance on the living who had harmed them. Death was not a termination but a change in form. The Celtic Otherworld, home of gods and fairies, later merged with the Christian realm of the dead. The dead themselves became confused with fairies. The land of the dead was often set in the western sea, sometimes as an unstable floating island. The dead were also imagined resting quietly in their graves, ready to come forth when the season was right. A controversial belief in reincarnation would explain the Celts' lack of interest in where the dead reside. Before finding another body, the dead could return to this world for a reason or on a certain day. Irish folktales tell of young mothers who return nightly to nurse their infants and lovers who come back to watch over a beloved. Most commonly, the dead returned on Samhain, the festival of November 1, when the veil between the worlds was thin. On Samhain, a murdered person could return for vengeance as readily as a thankful family member could grant a boon.
objective: The permeable boundary between the living and the dead, Celtic beliefs about the soul, and the return of the dead at Samhain.
key_results: The Celts believed in permeable boundaries between the living and the dead.
Caesar reported a continental Celtic belief in reincarnation.
Celtic burial shifted from grave goods to cremation and excarnation.
The dead returned most readily on Samhain, November 1.
